cues.text: The wind came off the moor a little after dawn.
By noon it had crossed Brannock Fell, flattening the grass for nineteen kilometres.
In the valley below, shepherds counted forty-eight ewes in the lee of the wall and waited for the rain.
In a workshop above the harbour, Ilse Marrowin shapes clay the way her teacher did.
A large bowl takes about three hours at the wheel,
and only one in twelve comes out of the kiln without a crack.
Every spring, the terns return to Kestrin Bay in great numbers.
Last season the wardens counted three hundred and twelve nesting pairs, the most in sixty years.
The first chicks hatch in late May, as the shallow water begins to warm.
The lighthouse at Tarnholm stands forty metres tall.
It still turns every night.
Snow came early to the high passes this year.
By October the drifts near the summit hut were two metres deep,
and the road stayed shut for eleven days.
In the square at Wendle Cross, a clock has kept time for two hundred and six years.
Its keeper climbs the tower every Sunday to wind it by hand.
The job takes forty turns of the old crank,
and in all that time the clock has stopped only four times.
On the south slope above the village, thirty-one hives stand in a single row.
The bees work the heather from July until the first hard frosts.
A strong colony can gather twenty kilograms of honey in a good summer,
though last year, after weeks of cold rain, most of the hives gave barely half of that.
The Harl Glacier has been measured every autumn since the survey began.
Each year a small team walks its lower edge and sets markers in the ice.
In the past fifty years the front has pulled back by more than nine hundred metres,
and the lake at its foot is now deep enough for boats.
The team expects it to double in size within twenty-five years.
Twice a day the tide pushes into the marshes at Saltmarrow, filling the channels one by one.
At the highest spring tides the water covers almost everything,
and only the sea wall and a few old posts stay dry.
Birds use the hours between the tides to feed.
In a single winter count, volunteers recorded fourteen thousand waders,
among them six kinds of plover and a lone spoonbill that stayed until March.
The railway to Velmora Pass climbs one thousand four hundred metres in just over seven kilometres.
That makes it one of the steepest lines of its kind in the world.
The carriages are pushed rather than pulled, so the engine is always below them on the slope.
In summer the trains run every hour from early morning until dusk,
and on busy weekends an extra carriage is added to each one.
In winter the line closes, and the track is left to the snow.
Every Thursday, the market at Pellwick Green fills the square before seven in the morning.
Farmers bring cheese, eggs and late apples from the hill farms up the valley,
and a handful still walk in from twelve kilometres away.
The weavers set up last, along the north side, where the daylight is best for showing colour.
A good blanket from their looms takes three weeks to make, and it will last a lifetime.
By noon the stalls are quiet, and by two in the afternoon the square is swept and empty again.
For most of its length the river Aldwen is too deep and too fast to cross on foot.
The only bridge for thirty kilometres stands at Ennick Mill, where the valley narrows between two walls of rock.
It was built from local stone by a crew of sixty-four masons,
and it took them the better part of nine years.
Floods have tested it many times since then, and it has been repaired more than once.
The worst of them rose six metres in a single night and carried away every tree along the bank,
but the bridge held, and by morning the first carts were crossing again.
